articles.title: haunted-shell: a tiny local ghost that whispers about my shell commands
articles.excerpt: Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine Submission 👻 This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4. haunted-shell is a tiny ghost that posses…
articles.body: Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine Submission 👻 This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4. What I Built haunted-shell is a tiny ghost that possesses my terminal. A shell hook watches each command I run, and a small open-weight model on my own machine whispers back one short, eerie comment. It never touches the command itself - it only watches and whispers. Real ghost output from the build's test runs. Each line below is a sample command string fed to the tool as text input (never executed), with an exit code passed alongside (2-core VM, model on CPU, no API key, no account): $ git push origin main 👻 your code is spreading like a plague... across the night $ rm -rf build/ 👻 ridding yourself of the unwanted...

articles.body: Most indie SaaS founders know they need monitoring but feel overwhelmed by the options and pricing. Sentry, PostHog, Highlight, and a dozen other tools each claim to be essential. In 2026, the monitoring landscape has consolidated into a few categories with clear price points. Here's the practical guide: what each category does, which tools to choose, and how to avoid paying for tools that solve problems you don't have. Quick Answer For indie SaaS in 2026, the essential monitoring stack is: Sentry for error tracking (free tier covers most indie projects), PostHog for product analytics and session replay (free tier: 1M events/month), and UptimeRobot or Better Uptime for server monitoring (free tier: 10 monitors). This covers the 80% of monitoring needs.

articles.title: The MCP header check is silently off for a tool your caller can't see
articles.excerpt: I sent one bad request to three MCP servers on mcp==2.3.0. Two answered 400 and named the argument the request was missing. One answered 200 and ran the tool anyway, with the argument still missing. T…
articles.body: I sent one bad request to three MCP servers on mcp==2.3.0 . Two answered 400 and named the argument the request was missing. One answered 200 and ran the tool anyway, with the argument still missing. That third server was the one whose tools/list did not advertise the tool I called. Nothing in its behaviour said "the check is off" — the call simply succeeded, and it succeeded because of a visibility rule, not because of anything I configured. The request MCP servers on the 2026-07-28 version can declare that a tool argument is mirrored into an HTTP header: { "properties" : { "job_id" : { "type" : "string" , "x-mcp-header" : "secret-tool-job-id" }}} The client then sends the value twice: once as Mcp-Param-secret-tool-job-id in the request headers, once inside arguments .

articles.title: Coding with AI is making me less tolerant of ambiguity
articles.excerpt: One thing I've noticed while coding with AI: a small ambiguity in the code can turn into a much bigger discussion than I expected. A nullable attribute is a good example. I see a field that can be nul…
articles.body: One thing I've noticed while coding with AI: a small ambiguity in the code can turn into a much bigger discussion than I expected. A nullable attribute is a good example. I see a field that can be null , and I may already know why. The assistant still has to work it out. Is the value missing? Is that a valid state? Should it use a default, skip something, or report an error? I've noticed it taking the cautious approach in situations like this. It asks more questions and adds checks. The result can look reasonable and still miss what I wanted. Take a simplified example: type Offer = { discountPercent : number | null ; }; What should the application display when the discount is null ? If it means there is no discount, showing the regular price makes sense.

articles.title: The Guardian denied both commands. It never read either one.
articles.excerpt: An MCP tool with one argument, script. I asked the OWASP Agent Control Standard (ACS) reference Guardian to judge two calls: echo ciao and echo rm -rf /. It denied both, for the same reason: {"decisio…
articles.body: An MCP tool with one argument, script . I asked the OWASP Agent Control Standard (ACS) reference Guardian to judge two calls: echo ciao and echo rm -rf / . It denied both, for the same reason: { "decision" : "deny" , "reasoning" : "mapping.yaml reads tool \" mcp__lab2__exec \" 's policy target from argument \" command \" , but this call sent no such argument (it sent: script)" , "reason_codes" :[ "evaluation_failed" ], "policy_references" :[]} The tool was already in the policy manifest, and the hook already sent its calls to the Guardian. It still needed a third entry before any rule read the command. Part 1 covers the setup and the method: Claude Code with its own model loop, the reference Guardian, the shipped hook, and every protocol frozen with its sha256 before it runs.

articles.title: LoabPron: a Notpron-style horror riddle haunted by a Gemma that lives on your computer
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine LoabPron is a love letter to Notpron, and to the strange corner of the internet it came from. In 2004 a…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built LoabPron is a love letter to Notpron , and to the strange corner of the internet it came from. The house that came before In 2004 a German developer, David Münnich, uploaded a few puzzle pages to a folder on his website that he had temporarily called notpron , a nod to an older online game called "This is not Porn". Thousands of people showed up and the name stuck. Notpron grew to 140 levels and called itself the hardest riddle on the internet. It earned it: by 2015 only about 34 people had been confirmed to reach the end, and by 2020 roughly a hundred, out of some twenty million visitors. Notpron was the best-known house in a whole neighbourhood of web riddles.

articles.title: Stunning solar eclipse photos reveal giant hole and mysterious 'smoke rings' in the sun's atmosphere
articles.excerpt: Solar eclipse photography provides a unique vista into the processes taking place in the sun's upper atmosphere.
articles.body: Newly released photographs of the sun captured during the Aug. 12 total solar eclipse reveal the sun's outer atmosphere in unprecedented detail. The images, released by researchers working as part of the Solar Wind Sherpas project coordinated by the University of Hawaii, also show rare structures in the solar wind known as smoke rings. Named for their resemblance to the circles blown by smokers, these vortices were first identified in solar eclipse photographs captured in 2008. The researchers had long struggled to explain the processes behind their formation. They now know the rings are a result of the temperature differences in the coronal plasma and spread along the sun 's magnetic lines deep into interplanetary space.

I play an obscene amount of soulslikes and sweaty action games, and although I largely enjoy my time facing off against these intentionally challenging gauntlets, one thing I’ve grown increasingly irritated by in recent years is something I’ve taken to calling the Scrub Tax . But what is the Scrub Tax exactly? Well, it can take many forms. Sometimes it’s a nearly minute-long walk back to the lair of the boss I’m trying to beat. articles.body: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.  AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 28, 1971: Britain launches its 1st satellite Prospero into space on a Black Arrow rocket
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. The satellite was named Prospero, but it was also known as the X-3. This wasn't Britain's first satellite , but it was the first and only one the British space program launched with one of its own rockets. The first six British satellites all launched from the United States on NASA rockets. Prospero launched on a carrier rocket called the Black Arrow. The Prospero mission was the fourth and final flight of a Black Arrow rocket . Prospero was designed to study how the environment in space affects communications satellites. It tested things solar cells and telemetry systems, and even had a micrometeoroid detector that would determine small particles in space posed a threat to the spacecraft.
